strengths: Viewed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than primarily an Algorithms/General paper, the work addresses an important problem: large-scale supervision for iterative, spatially grounded visual reasoning. The 489K-example VISREASON collection spans text/document understanding, fine-grained recognition, general VQA, and spatial relations, while VISREASON-PRO adds 165K depth-informed examples.

The global-to-local annotation format—scene description, region of interest, rationale, and optional iterative zoom—offers useful process supervision beyond answer-only VQA. Adaptive zooming is practically motivated and the paper provides generation algorithms, prompts, and substantial implementation detail.

The reported empirical coverage is broad. VISREASON-PRO-7B improves the Visual-CoT macro-average from 0.770 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B to 0.807, and VISREASON-7B improves V* from the strongest listed baseline score of 0.597 to 0.619. The paper also includes localization, pseudo-depth grounding, ablations, and a blinded human evaluation.

The authors appropriately acknowledge that pseudo-3D grounding and localization remain difficult: even their best grounded ratio is only 0.276 and IoU@0.75 is 0.23. Reporting these modest absolute values is informative.
weaknesses: The central benchmark evidence is insufficiently independent. VISREASON-PRO is both a training resource and the basis of the proposed benchmark, but the manuscript does not clearly specify benchmark size, train/test construction, deduplication, or image/question disjointness. Evaluation uses official validation splits of the same source datasets from which training examples are generated. Without an explicit leakage audit and independently curated test set, the reported gains may reflect adaptation to source data and generator conventions.

The localization comparison is not controlled fairly. The authors' models use a refined multi-round RoI, whereas baselines are explicitly restricted to a single-step box. This confounds learned capability with inference-time interaction and computation. Moreover, Table 3 evaluates against the final generated CoT RoI rather than clearly against an independently annotated object box, favoring models trained to imitate the dataset's synthetic trajectories.

The claimed 3D grounding is based entirely on monocular pseudo-depth, segmentation, and generated questions, with no validation against real depth or human spatial judgments. Ground-truth objects are parsed from generated reference rationales, object matching is exact lowercased-name matching, and IoU/depth error are averaged only over matched objects. These design choices make the metrics brittle and can reward selective grounding; the very low grounded ratios further weaken the claim of strong 3D reasoning.

The rationales are post-hoc and heavily privileged: generation receives the correct answer and ground-truth box, and every predicted RoI is forcibly expanded to contain that box. Thus, the pipeline guarantees spatial consistency mechanically but does not establish that descriptions and rationales are faithful reasoning traces. No systematic human audit of annotation correctness, ambiguity, depth ordering, or rationale faithfulness is reported; some displayed examples already contain questionable scene descriptions.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed ingredients. VISREASON-PRO adds data, stronger GPT-4.1-Mini generation, depth cues, richer rationales, and an additional training stage simultaneously. There are no size- and compute-matched controls for single-round versus multi-round supervision, pseudo-depth versus no depth, or generated rationales versus boxes alone. The external evaluation also omits the essential Qwen2.5-VL backbone, and VISREASON-PRO performs worse than VISREASON on both MME and V*, tempering the generalization claim.

Several protocol contradictions materially impair reproducibility. The main text states learning rates of 2e-5 for the language model/projector and 2e-6 for the ViT, while the supplement reports 1e-5 and a frozen vision tower. The main text describes an additional epoch on the full combined datasets, whereas the supplement says the PRO stage uses only VISREASON-PRO. The main evaluation description uses an LLM judge, but the supplement describes normalized exact-match accuracy. It is therefore unclear how the principal numbers were obtained.

The human study is underreported: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement measures, sampling details, or per-method assignment counts. Dataset licensing, consent/privacy implications of aggregating source images, GPT-generation parameters and cost, filtering rejection rates, and a concrete release artifact are also not adequately documented. Because dataset quality and benchmark validity are the core contribution, these are substantive rather than merely presentational omissions.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and offers a potentially useful resource: 489K process-supervised examples across document understanding, fine-grained recognition, VQA, and spatial reasoning, including a 165K depth-aware portion. I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than the default Algorithms/General type, so its scale, annotation validity, benchmark design, and documentation carry more weight than algorithmic novelty. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/958797a482ee4eb59b500d571044b3cb/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The global-to-local zoom interface is intuitive, relevant to small-object and text-heavy tasks, and specified with useful algorithmic and prompting details in the supplement.

Experiments cover 11 constituent Visual-CoT datasets, two external benchmarks, localization and depth metrics, ablations, and a human evaluation. The trained 7B models improve the reported Visual-CoT average from 0.770 for Qwen2.5-VL to 0.791/0.807, with especially notable gains on fine-grained recognition and Open Images.
The authors expose important remaining difficulty rather than hiding it: even their best localization results are only 0.34 at IoU@0.5 and 0.23 at IoU@0.75.
weaknesses: The dataset does not convincingly contain faithful reasoning. Its rationales are generated while the model is given the answer and ground-truth box, and every predicted RoI is forcibly expanded to include that box. Consequently, the traces are post-hoc answer-conditioned explanations, while localization correctness is partly guaranteed by construction. Claims of “human-like,” faithful reasoning, reduced shortcut learning, and interpretability are therefore substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

VISREASON-PRO and its benchmark are circularly validated. Questions, target boxes, rationales, object depths, and benchmark references are produced from the same monocular-depth/segmentation and GPT-based pipeline. Evaluation measures agreement with these synthetic pseudo-labels rather than genuine 3D geometry. There is no evaluation against measured depth, human-verified spatial relations, or an independent 3D benchmark, and no quantitative audit of pseudo-depth, generated-QA, or rationale error rates.

The localization comparison is not fair: the proposed models receive iterative crops and are scored using their last multi-round box, whereas baselines are explicitly restricted to a single-step box. This confounds training supervision with extra inference interaction and visual resolution. All models should receive the same tool interface and round/pixel budget, with separate comparisons for one-shot and iterative settings.

The answer-evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 5 says an LLM judge assigns continuous scores, Figure 15 gives a GPT similarity-grading prompt, but Supplement Section 9 instead describes normalized exact-match accuracy. The judge model, calibration results, stochastic variance, and per-example outputs are not reported. Thus the principal numbers in Table 2 are not reproducibly defined.

Training documentation contains consequential contradictions: the main paper gives learning rates of 2e-5 for the language model/projector and 2e-6 for the vision encoder, whereas the supplement reports 1e-5 and says the vision tower is frozen. The appendix simultaneously describes LoRA adaptation and the language model/projector as fully trainable. Code, data download details, seeds, run variance, and checkpoint availability are also absent.

The ablation does not cleanly establish causality. Table 6 does not clearly define the five training conditions or control for dataset size and compute, and adding both dataset components without adaptive zoom performs worse than several simpler conditions. “Pro” changes multiple factors simultaneously—source distribution, annotation model, rationale detail, generated questions, and pseudo-depth—so improvements cannot be attributed specifically to depth-aware supervision.

External generalization is mixed rather than consistently positive: VISREASON-PRO is worse than VISREASON on both MME (0.777 vs. 0.808) and V* (0.603 vs. 0.619), and remains below InternVL on MME. No uncertainty, repeated runs, or statistical testing is supplied for relatively small aggregate differences.

The human study is inadequately documented. It reports 30 raters and 20 items per method but omits recruitment, expertise, assignment design, rating instructions, randomization, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, significance tests, and whether raters saw model identities or rationale formats. It therefore cannot substantiate the paper’s strong faithfulness claims.

Because training and testing reuse the same Visual-CoT family and underlying source datasets, a deduplication and contamination audit is essential but missing. The paper also does not sufficiently discuss source-dataset licenses, redistribution rights, privacy concerns in document images, annotation costs, release format, or model/API versioning. These omissions are particularly serious for a paper whose main contribution is a large derived dataset.

Presentation quality is below publication readiness: terminology alternates between RoI and AoI, there are errors such as “Spatial Relatio,” “gruounding,” and “Blod,” some examples contain inconsistent coordinates or dubious descriptions, and Figure 6’s caption refers to a VisCoT comparison that is not clearly shown. Overall, the resource has promise, but the circular construction, weak annotation validation, unfair benchmark comparison, and contradictory evaluation/training protocols prevent a convincing scientific case in the current form.

strengths: This is a timely and potentially valuable Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. VISREASON provides 489K process-supervised examples across text/document understanding, fine-grained recognition, general VQA, and spatial-relation reasoning; VISREASON-PRO adds 165K examples with pseudo-depth and segmentation-derived grounding.

The global-to-local zoom-and-verify format is intuitive and practically useful. It couples textual rationales with explicit regions of interest and allows models to spend additional visual resolution only when needed.

The empirical results are broadly encouraging. VISREASON-PRO-7B improves the Visual-CoT macro-average from 0.770 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B to 0.807, with particularly strong gains on CUB and Open Images. It also improves V* performance and leads the reported RoI and pseudo-3D grounding evaluations.

The paper evaluates multiple aspects of the contribution: answer quality on 11 source datasets, transfer to MME and V*, RoI localization, depth-aware grounding, component ablations, and a blinded human evaluation with 30 raters. This breadth supports the practical relevance of the resource.

The supplement supplies generation algorithms, prompts, training configurations, and evaluation protocols, substantially improving clarity and reproducibility. The paper is generally well organized and provides useful qualitative examples.

The work does not merely introduce synthetic annotations: it demonstrates that training on them improves a strong 7B backbone and makes the resulting reasoning more spatially explicit. This is a meaningful contribution to visual reasoning even though the model architecture itself is largely standard.
weaknesses: The claimed faithfulness and human-like nature of the chains is not fully established. Rationales are generated while conditioning on the answer, and every proposed RoI is forcibly expanded to contain the ground-truth box. Consequently, the traces are post-hoc, answer-aware explanations whose localization success is partly guaranteed by construction, rather than independent demonstrations of the reasoning needed to discover an answer.

Dataset quality validation is limited relative to the scale and synthetic nature of the resource. There is no systematic human audit reporting error rates for questions, answers, rationales, boxes, or depth relations. Some displayed examples contain questionable intermediate descriptions, underscoring the need for stratified quality estimates across domains and reasoning rounds.

The VISREASON-PRO ablation changes several factors simultaneously: generator strength, source distribution, rationale detail, synthetic QA generation, and depth supervision. It therefore does not isolate whether the gains arise specifically from 3D cues. A size-matched control without depth and an evaluation restricted to genuinely depth-dependent questions would make the central 3D claim much stronger.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. In the RoI benchmark, the proposed models receive iterative zooming while baselines are restricted to a single box, so Tables 3–4 conflate training quality with inference interface. Table 2 also mixes results taken from prior work with reproduced results without identifying each case or reporting uncertainty. Broader comparisons with recent visual-search/reasoning systems would help.

The new benchmark is generated from the same pipeline and source distribution used for training, with pseudo-depth serving as ground truth. Exact name-based object matching and depth error computed only over matched objects can be brittle or selectively favorable. Clear train/validation image deduplication, independent human verification, and evaluation on real depth or independently annotated relations are needed.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies: the main paper states learning rates of 2e-5 for the language model/projector and 2e-6 for the vision encoder, whereas the supplement reports a frozen vision tower and a 1e-5 learning rate. The description of LoRA on all trainable modules also sits uneasily with the statement that the projector and language model are fully trainable. These should be reconciled, along with the exact representation of intermediate crop images during SFT.

The human study omits important details such as rater assignment, number of ratings per item, agreement, variance or confidence intervals, and significance testing. Dataset release details are also incomplete: no concrete release link, artifact specification, source-license analysis, or discussion of privacy risks in document/receipt imagery is provided.

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence warrants. The reported results support improved task performance and spatially explicit outputs, but do not by themselves demonstrate reduced shortcut learning, genuine cognitive reasoning, or faithful internal reasoning. These claims should be narrowed or tested with counterfactual and rationale-intervention experiments.

strengths: The work is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: its central asset is a large 489K-example, multi-domain visual-reasoning corpus, including a 165K-example subset with pseudo-depth annotations, rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm. Under that framing, the scale, breadth, and process-level RoI supervision are potentially valuable to the community.

The dataset format is useful and comparatively rich: examples contain multi-round descriptions, localized regions, rationales, and final answers, while VisReason-Pro additionally provides segmentation-derived boxes and ordinal-depth cues. The adaptive zoom-and-verify interface is intuitive and relevant to small-object, fine-grained, and document tasks.

The empirical package is extensive. It includes Qwen2.5-VL-7B experiments, a second InternVL backbone, direct-answer versus multi-round inference, localization and depth-grounding measurements, source-removal analysis, external benchmarks, and human evaluation. VisReason-Pro improves the weighted Visual-CoT score from 0.770 to 0.802, with particularly large gains on CUB and Open Images.

Reproducibility information is stronger than usual: the supplement supplies generation prompts, algorithms, training configurations, evaluation parsing details, and a 2,200-example human audit with confidence intervals. The audit reports 99.1% answer consistency and 98.5% target containment, while the GPT-based evaluator is calibrated against human scores.
weaknesses: The generated chains are answer- and target-conditioned rather than independently discovered: generation receives the short answer and ground-truth box, and every predicted RoI is explicitly expanded to contain that box. The final justification again receives the answer and box. Consequently, these traces are post-hoc demonstrations guaranteed to retain the target, which substantially weakens claims that they capture faithful or human-like reasoning, discourage shortcuts, or verify the model's actual inference process.

The evidence for generalization is weak and strongly source-dependent. Evaluation uses validation sets from the same source families represented in training, and most of the overall improvement is concentrated in CUB (+0.150) and Open Images (+0.307). Results decline on VSR and all five Text/Doc datasets; on the second backbone, the total improvement is only 0.002, with sizable losses on GQA (-0.140), VSR (-0.095), and Visual7W (-0.059). The source-removal experiment itself confirms that gains depend heavily on matched domain sources.

The ablations do not cleanly identify the value of depth, richer rationales, annotator strength, or multi-round supervision. VisReason-Pro changes the data source/content, GPT annotator, pseudo-depth inputs, number of examples, and training duration together. Likewise, adaptive zoom changes inference behavior and computation. Controlled comparisons against answer-only, box-only, single-round, shuffled-rationale, and equally trained non-depth variants are needed.

The evaluation description contains consequential inconsistencies. The supplement alternately describes exact-match accuracy and GPT-4o-mini scoring, and states macro-averaging even though the main paper and tables state sample-size-weighted averaging. Moreover, the localization benchmark compares against generated final-round CoT RoIs, while the 3D metric uses pseudo-depth and exact textual-name matching, averages box/depth quality only over matched objects, and attains a low grounded ratio of 0.276. These choices limit the strength of the claimed grounding and 3D conclusions.

The annotation audit reveals an important domain-specific limitation that is understated by aggregate numbers: Text/Doc rationale necessity and faithfulness are only 70.9% and 71.9%, respectively. Details needed to interpret both audits and the 30-rater user study—rater expertise, assignment design, inter-rater agreement, filtering, and statistical significance of method differences—are insufficient.

Despite presenting the resource as a release, the manuscript does not provide a concrete repository, immutable dataset artifact, license, or a clear discussion of redistribution rights for the many constituent datasets and generated derivatives. These are important reproducibility and attribution requirements for a dataset paper. Overall, the scale and potential utility make the decision close, but the circular construction/evaluation and insufficiently controlled evidence currently favor borderline rejection.

strengths: As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the paper addresses a relevant problem: scalable supervision for iterative, spatially grounded visual reasoning. The proposed resource is large (489K examples, including a 165K depth-augmented component) and spans document/text, fine-grained recognition, general VQA, and spatial reasoning.

The global-to-local interaction format, with explicit RoIs and adaptive zooming, is intuitive and potentially useful for small objects, fine details, and text. The paper provides generation algorithms, prompts, training configurations, and inference procedures in substantial detail.

The authors conduct useful validation beyond aggregate answer accuracy, including RoI localization, pseudo-depth grounding, a 2,200-example annotation audit, human evaluation, evaluator calibration, direct-QA comparisons, and transfer to an InternVL backbone.

Some empirical improvements are substantial: on the source-matched Visual-CoT evaluation, VisReason-Pro improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 0.681 to 0.831 on CUB and from 0.498 to 0.805 on Open Images. The human study also favors the proposed models on grounded faithfulness and stepwise clarity.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges pseudo-depth noise, extra inference cost, localization-error cascades, and the lack of a zoom-out or recovery mechanism. The source-removal experiment is also unusually candid about dependence on domain-relevant training data.
weaknesses: The construction procedure fundamentally weakens the claimed faithfulness of the reasoning supervision. The generator is given the ground-truth short answer, and every predicted RoI is mechanically expanded with the ground-truth box via AdjustRoI/AdjustAoI. The final justification is likewise generated with the answer and ground-truth box. These are post-hoc, answer-conditioned explanations rather than evidence that the intermediate reasoning process discovered the answer or target faithfully.

The central experimental gains are not isolated from ordinary in-domain supervised fine-tuning. The paper lacks a matched answer-only or single-step QA fine-tuning baseline using exactly the same images, questions, answers, training budget, and generated Pro questions. Consequently, the results do not establish that multi-round CoT rationales, rather than exposure to task-specific QA data and target boxes, cause the improvements.

Generalization is weak. Under direct-QA inference, the proposed checkpoint averages 0.769 versus 0.770 for the base Qwen model. Multi-round improvements are concentrated in CUB and Open Images, while VSR falls from 0.705 to 0.654 and several document tasks regress. InternVL transfer changes the overall score only from 0.738 to 0.740 and causes large drops on GQA (-0.140), VSR (-0.095), and Visual7W (-0.059). The source-removal ablation further shows severe dependence on source-domain coverage.

The VisReason-Pro localization comparison is procedurally confounded: trained models may emit and refine multiple zoom boxes, whereas single-step baselines are instructed to produce one box. This compares both training and inference interfaces simultaneously, so the paper cannot attribute the advantage specifically to better localization ability. Absolute performance also remains low at 0.34 IoU@0.5 and 0.23 IoU@0.75.

The pseudo-3D benchmark has serious validity limitations. Its reference objects, boxes, and depths are derived from monocular estimators and generated rationales rather than independently verified 3D ground truth. Objects are matched by exact lowercased names, and IoU/depth error is averaged only over matched objects, introducing vocabulary and selection biases that favor models trained on the annotation format. Even the proposed model grounds only 27.6% of reference objects and reaches mean IoU 0.278.

Claims of human-like reasoning, interpretability, and reduced shortcut learning are substantially stronger than the evidence. Generated rationales can merely verbalize supplied answers and boxes; no causal-faithfulness test, rationale intervention, counterfactual evaluation, or comparison against non-rationale supervision is provided. The audit's 70.9% rationale necessity and 71.9% rationale faithfulness for Text/Doc further qualify the broad claims.

The human study is under-specified despite its strong use in the conclusions: only 20 sampled items per method are reported, without confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, assignment details, or the complete rating protocol. Similar annotator-count, adjudication, and agreement details are missing for the dataset audit.

Reproducibility and dataset governance are incomplete for a dataset paper. No accessible dataset/code URL, concrete release status, license, inherited-source licensing analysis, redistribution terms, or discussion of privacy and annotation-related societal risks is provided. The commercial generators are identified only as GPT-4.1 Nano/Mini rather than immutable versions with complete decoding settings and generation costs.

There is an internal reporting inconsistency: the main paper and tables describe the overall Visual-CoT score as a sample-size-weighted mean, whereas Supplement Sec. C states that per-dataset accuracies are macro-averaged. Baseline results are also described as either copied or reproduced without identifying which results follow which procedure.

strengths: The submission is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: it introduces a large resource with 489K multi-round, RoI-grounded examples across four domains, plus a 165K depth-informed subset. This scale, structured supervision, and domain coverage constitute a useful computer-vision contribution even though the learning algorithm itself is largely standard SFT with adaptive cropping.

The global-to-local formulation is intuitive and practically relevant for small objects, fine-grained recognition, document details, and spatial relations. The dataset supplies explicit intermediate regions rather than only free-form rationales, making its supervision more inspectable and potentially reusable for tool-using or agentic MLLMs.

The empirical results are encouraging. VisReason-Pro improves the Qwen2.5-VL-7B weighted Visual-CoT score from 0.770 to 0.802, with particularly large gains on CUB (0.681 to 0.831) and Open Images (0.498 to 0.805). RoI localization, grounded-ratio, and human-evaluation results also favor the proposed training.

The evaluation is broader and more candid than is typical for dataset-generation work: it includes a second backbone, inference-format controls, component ablations, external MME and V* evaluation, a 2,200-example annotation audit with confidence intervals, and calibration of the GPT-based evaluator against human ratings.

The paper clearly acknowledges important boundaries: pseudo-depth is ordinal rather than metric 3D, direct-QA can be preferable for short-answer tasks, source-domain coverage drives much of the benefit, and iterative cropping can suffer cascading localization failures. The supplement provides algorithms, prompts, training configurations, and parsing details that substantially aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central evidence does not establish broad source-independent generalization. Training and evaluation use different splits of the same underlying source families, and the source-removal experiment causes very large drops. On the second backbone, the overall gain is only 0.738 to 0.740, with regressions on GQA, VSR, Visual7W, and document tasks. External direct-QA results are essentially unchanged. The contribution is therefore better supported as useful domain-specialized supervision than as a general improvement in visual reasoning.

The generated chains are post-hoc rationalizations rather than independently verified reasoning trajectories: the annotator is given the answer, and every proposed RoI is forcibly expanded to contain the ground-truth box. This makes containment partly true by construction and weakens claims that the rationales are faithful, human-like, or that they discourage shortcut learning. Human-rated plausibility does not demonstrate causal reliance on the stated reasoning steps.

The VisReason-Pro localization benchmark is somewhat circular. Its reference RoIs are generated final-round CoT regions rather than purely human-annotated target boxes, while the proposed models are explicitly trained to reproduce this format. Baselines use single-step native grounding prompts whereas the proposed model receives an iterative zoom interface. Thus the modest absolute localization results (IoU@0.5 of 0.34 and IoU@0.75 of 0.23) should be interpreted cautiously.

The 3D-grounding evaluation mixes geometric ability with output-format compliance. Objects are matched by lowercased textual names, errors are computed only on matched objects, and the proposed model was trained to serialize boxes and pseudo-depth values in precisely this format. A controlled evaluation using fixed object identities, human-verified ordinal relations, and penalties for missing objects would make the geometric claim more convincing.

There are several protocol inconsistencies that should be corrected. The supplement describes normalized exact-match accuracy and a macro-average, whereas the tables describe GPT-4o-mini scores and sample-size-weighted averages. The user study also lacks sufficient information about item sampling, assignment of the 30 raters, inter-rater agreement, and statistical significance.

The promised release is scientifically important but the manuscript does not provide a concrete repository, dataset license, release status, or a detailed discussion of the licenses and redistribution constraints of the many constituent datasets. Given the use of automatically generated rationales and document images, data governance and failure/bias analysis deserve more attention.
